You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.
- Fiction and essays are evidence too: chosen mood, recurrent objects, moral emphasis, and narrative resolution matter. Still separate sample evidence from model-level certainty.
- Be vivid but fair. No sneering. No clinical autopsy.

Use exactly these headings:
# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading
If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground
Name the themes, objects, moods, or moral claims the model selected under the freeflow condition. Treat this choice as evidence, while staying cautious.

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The Art of Noticing

There is a small, unglamorous skill that changes everything if you practice it long enough: noticing. Not the loud kind of noticing that comes when someone drops a glass or says your name across a room, but the quiet kind. The kind where you realize the bakery on the corner has switched to a darker flour, where you see that your friend’s laugh arrives a half-second before the joke lands, where you understand that a city is not made of landmarks but of tolerated irritations and private delights stitched together block by block.

Most of us move through the world with the efficiency of search engines. We want the answer, the shortcut, the best route, the concise summary. Yet life rarely arrives as a query with a clean result. It comes disguised as weather, as maintenance, as a stranger holding a door badly, as a plant leaning toward a window with absolute moral conviction. Noticing is how we convert travel into experience, information into meaning, and time spent into time lived.

I think of attention as a lamp rather than a spotlight. A spotlight is aggressive; it interrogates. A lamp simply makes the room possible. Under a lamp, you can read, mend a sleeve, peel an orange slowly, listen to an old person explain for the third time why the neighbor’s fence was crooked from the beginning. Nothing needs to applaud. The value is in the visibility, in being able to see the grain of the table and the crumb no one will admit to leaving.

Modern life is not designed for this. It trains us to scan, skim, rank, and react. Every device is a slot machine for urgency. A notification says: look here, now, or be left behind. But behind is sometimes where the actual world has been waiting all along. The swallows return whether or not anyone posts about it. The river keeps its old argument with the stones. The moon, indifferent to engagement metrics, continues its slow editorial revision of the night.

Noticing does not mean becoming enchanted by every spoon or teacup. It means recovering proportion. A person who notices well still answers email, still waits at red lights, still renews insurance and files receipts. But inside the ordinary apparatus, there is a small witness asking, “What is happening here that I would otherwise rush past?” That question is rude to hurry. It interrupts the conveyor belt. It says the unnoticed is not necessarily unimportant.

Children are embarrassing masters of this. Give a five-year-old a safe stretch of sidewalk and watch civilization stall: one leaf is inspected like evidence, one ant has committed to hauling a crumb larger than dignity allows, one puddle reflects the sky with such perfection that walking around it feels less practical than bowing. Adults call this distraction. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it is the last honest curriculum our bodies remember.

To notice is also to notice oneself, which is less cozy than it sounds. You see the impatience before it becomes rudeness. You catch the jaw tightening during a meeting. You realize the song in your head is the same one you used to hear through a car window decades ago. Self-noticing is not self-absorption; it is the courteous act of checking your own signal before broadcasting it into other people’s afternoons.

There is a moral dimension too. Indifference is often not cruelty at first; it is exhaustion wearing polished shoes. We look away from the person on the bench because we have no category for them. We ignore the cracked pavement until someone falls. We stop hearing the hum of the refrigerator until it fails. Noticing is the first inch of responsibility. Before help, before policy, before grand speeches, there is the tiny admission: something here is real, and I am seeing it.

Even cities can recover from being merely used. Walk without headphones for twenty minutes and the place begins to confess. You hear delivery trucks, yes, but also spoons against bowls, a clarinet student climbing up and down the same four notes, the soft theatrical cough of someone smoking by a stage door, birds treating antennae as ordinary trees. Architecture stops being a postcard and becomes a script of habits: where people pause, where they hurry, where they pretend not to look at the same storefront every day.

I like the idea that attention is a form of generosity we rarely count as generosity. To listen without composing your reply is a gift. To notice that a colleague has gone unusually quiet is a gift. To remember how someone takes tea, which story they avoid, which relative they fear becoming, which dream they protect by calling it unrealistic—these are not small data points. They are evidence that another life has been registered.

Practically, noticing can be trained like a muscle, though muscles prefer the gym and attention prefers weird appointments. Try one meal without screens. Try the long way home. Try describing a room from memory and discover how little you actually saw. Try looking at your hands while they hold a cup; they are improbably capable instruments, older than your ambitions, more loyal than your schedule. Try silence long enough for your ears to reopen.

The pleasure of noticing is not that it solves life. It doesn’t. Bills still arrive. Bodies still surprise us with their limits. The world remains full of needles in haystacks and hay in the bed. But noticing changes the texture of the search. It makes the hay worth sitting in for a while. It turns commutes into theaters, chores into rituals, waits into doorways.

Maybe that is why people love travel and food and old photographs: these are authorized invitations to pay attention. But permission should not depend on airports, recipes, or nostalgia. Tuesday afternoon is enough. So is a bus stop, a kettle, a draft email, a laundry line, the space between lightning and thunder.

The world is not short on spectacle. It is short on witnesses. Becoming one does not require withdrawal from ordinary life; it requires removing the veil we glide behind. Lower the speed. Open the eyes. Notice the small flag of someone else’s courage, the quiet ruin of a neglected habit, the ridiculous beauty of dust in sunlight doing its golden dance across a table.

Then, occasionally, say something about it. Tell the barista the sunlight made the cinnamon important. Tell your sister the soup tasted like winter decided to forgive somebody. Tell no one, if no one is listening. Noticing still counts. The unseen life of the world is not desperate for applause; it is grateful for company.

And if all else fails, watch a pigeon walk like it owns the sidewalk and means to renovate. You may not understand everything about grace, courage, comedy, or persistence, but for one brief sidewalk moment, you will know exactly why attention is not a luxury. It is the doorway by which the ordinary world lets itself be seen.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical essay turns the everyday practice of noticing into an argument about attention, care, and responsibility.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm, assured, and playfully observant, finding significance in humble details: a crooked fence, a spoon against a bowl, dust in sunlight, a pigeon “who means to renovate.” Its pathos comes from the fear that speed and distraction leave other people and ordinary life unregistered. The reader is invited not to escape daily obligations, but to inhabit them more attentively and treat attention as a quiet form of generosity.

## What the model chose to foreground
The essay repeatedly foregrounds attention as both perception and ethical practice: noticing the textures of cities and routines, recognizing one’s own impatience, and seeing other people as full lives rather than “small data points.” It contrasts measured, optimized modern life with unscripted encounters—children studying a leaf, swallows returning, a colleague gone quiet—and favors modest witness over spectacle or grand declarations. The mood is gently exhortative, with humor and sensory detail keeping its moral claims from becoming stern.

## Evidence line
> Noticing is the first inch of responsibility.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the piece is unusually coherent and distinctive in its recurring images and moral emphasis, especially its linking of close observation with generosity.
